```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(knitr)
library(quarto)
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = './')
```

# Data description

The aim of this pilot study is to compare three microsampling devices profiles
with conventional liquid samples, plasma and whole blood, in an untargeted LCMS
analysis. The final objective is to determine which device perform a similar
profile to plasma, gold standard sample, generating less artefacts. For this,
there will be a qualitative comparison (number of features, metabolites
annotated) and a semi-quantitative comparison (intensity and statistical
differences).

[**Samples of study**]{.underline}

The samples used in this study were venous blood samples collected from 10
healthy individuals ( 5 men and 5 women) in EDTA tubes. Part of this blood was
used as whole blood sample, part was used for plasma extraction and part was
spiked in devices to simulate sample collection through fingerprick.

Total number of samples: 66

double blanks:

-   BLANK_001(beginning)

-   BLANK_002 (beginning)

-   BLANK_003 (beginning)

-   BLANK_END

Blanks from devices:

-   Blank_W

-   Blank_M

-   Blank_C

Randomise Samples:

-   10 x WHATMAN

-   10 x MITRA

-   10 x CAPITAINER

-   10 x PLASMA

-   10 x BLOOD

-   10 x QCs

[**Sample preparation and acquisition**]{.underline}

Samples were treated H2O and IPA for protein precipitation and lipids
extraction. Then extracts were analysed in a UPLC-ESI-QTOF system (Synapt-G2S)
(Waters Corporation) using resolution mode for MS1 and FastDDA for MS2 data.

## Define colors

We will define colors for each of the sample groups based on their sample group
using the *RColorBrewer* package:

```{r define-colors, include=FALSE}
#' Define colors for dataset
col_device <- brewer.pal(7, name = "Set3")
names(col_device) <- unique(sampleData(lcms1)$device)
col_sample <- col_device[sampleData(lcms1)$device]
col_qc <- brewer.pal(10, name = "Set3")

#' Define colors for dataset without blanks
col_noblank <- col_sample[names(col_sample)!= "BLANK"]

#' Define colors for samples
col_sampleonly <- col_sample[!(names(col_sample) %in% c("BLANK", "QC"))]

#' Define colors for dataset with different blank type
col_blank_type <- brewer.pal(12, name ="Set3")
names(col_blank_type) <- unique(sampleData(lcms1)$blank_type)
```

The MS data of this experiment is stored as a *`Spectra` object* (from the
`r Biocpkg("Spectra")` Bioconductor package) within the `MsExperiment` object
and can be accessed using `spectra()` function. Each element in this object is a
spectrum.

```{r spectra-objec, eval = FALSE}
#' Access Spectra Object
spectra(lcms1)
```

We can also summarize the number of spectra and their respective MS level. We
only have MS1 here.

```{r number_spectra, eval = FALSE}
#' Count the number of spectra with a specific MS level per file.
spectra(lcms1) |>
    msLevel() |>
    split(fromFile(lcms1)) |>
    lapply(table) |>
    do.call(what = cbind)
```

The present data set thus contains only MS1 data, which is ideal for
quantification of the signal. Also all the samples seem to have a similar number
of scans, which is good.

As another example, we below determine the retention time range for the entire
data set.

```{r rt-range}
#' Retention time range for entire dataset
spectra(lcms1) |>
    rtime() |>
    range()
```

Data obtained from LC-MS experiments are typically analyzed along the retention
time axis, while MS data is organized by spectrum, orthogonal to the retention
time axis.

# Data visualization and general quality assessment

Effective visualization is paramount for inspecting and assessing the quality of
MS data. For a general overview of our LC-MS data, we can:

-   Combine all mass peaks from all (MS1) spectra of a sample into a single
    spectrum in which each mass peak then represents the maximum signal of all
    mass peaks with a similar *m/z*. This spectrum might then be called **Base
    Peak Spectrum (BPS)**, providing information on the most abundant ions of a
    sample.
-   Aggregate mass peak intensities for each spectrum, resulting in the **Base
    Peak Chromatogram (BPC)**. The BPC shows the highest measured intensity for
    each distinct retention time (hence spectrum) and is thus orthogonal to the
    BPS.
-   Sum the mass peak intensities for each spectrum to create a **Total Ion
    Chromatogram (TIC).**
-   **Compare the BPS** of all samples in an experiment to evaluate similarity
    of their ion content.
-   **Compare the BPC** of all samples in an experiment to identify samples with
    similar or dissimilar chromatographic signal.

In addition to such general data evaluation and visualization, it is also
crucial to investigate **specific signal** of e.g. internal standards or
compounds/ions known to be present in the samples. By providing a reliable
reference, internal standards help achieve consistent and accurate analytical
results.

## Chromatographic Data Visualization: BPC and TIC

```{r bpc1, eval=FALSE}
#| fig-cap: "Figure 1. BPC before rt filtering of all samples colored by device."
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#' Extract and plot BPC for full data
bpc <- chromatogram(lcms1, aggregationFun = "max")

plot(bpc, col = paste0(col_sample, 80), main = "BPC", lwd = 1.5)
grid()
legend("topright", col = col_device, legend = names(col_device), 
       lty = 1, lwd = 2, horiz = FALSE,
       bty = "n", cex = 0.9)
```

After filtering, we realised the Heatmap had a different layout. At the
beginning it seems the Capitainer devices were different to the rest. However,
now it seems all devices are grouped together. That is way, I want to plot the
heatmap again to check this variation is due to filtering or due to another
modification I am not aware of .

We can see separation of samples per group. Only Blood, Whatman and Mitra
samples are mixed, probably due to the same blood extraction. However,
Capitainer is separated from the others. This disappears if we filter the rt and
plot the heatmap again.

```{r heatmap, eval=FALSE}
#| fig-cap: "Figure 2. Heatmap of TIC similarities before filtering."
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Show the code"
#' Total ion chromatogram
tic <- chromatogram(lcms1, aggregationFun = "sum") |>
  bin(binSize = 2)

#' Calculate similarity (Pearson correlation) between BPCs
ticmap <- do.call(cbind, lapply(tic, intensity)) |>
  cor()

#' Add sample names as rownames and colnames
rownames(ticmap) <- colnames(ticmap) <- sampleData(lcms1)$sample_name
ann <- data.frame(device = sampleData(lcms1)[, "device"])
rownames(ann) <- rownames(ticmap)

#' Plot heatmap
pheatmap(ticmap, annotation_col = ann,
         annotation_colors = list(device = col_device),
         show_rownames = FALSE, show_colnames = FALSE)
```

### Known compounds

Throughout the entire process, it is crucial to have reference points within the
dataset, such as well-known ions, useful for the visualization of data
throughout the entire analysis. Most experiments nowadays include internal
standards (IS). In this case, no standards were spiked, so 12 known compounds
were selected from the National Phenome Center library. This library was built
using the same LCMS method and metabolites were annotated using standards
(<https://github.com/phenomecentre/npc-open-lcms/blob/main/LC-MS%20Metabolite%20Annotations/LPOS_ROI_V_5_1_2.csv>).

-   PC(16:0/18:2)
-   LPC(0:0/18:2)
-   PC(18:0/18:2)
-   Cholesterol
-   LPC(0:0/16:0)
-   LPC(18:0/0:0)
-   LPC(18:1/0:0)
-   LPC(O-18:0/0:0)
-   SM(d16:1/16:0)
-   PC(16:0/20:4)
-   PC(16:0/16:0)
-   SM(d18:2/24:0)

We also plot all of them and save the images locally to check manually.

```{r EIC_extract_for_internal_standard1}
#' get the list
intern_standard <- read_xlsx("standard_compound_addition.xlsx") |> 
  as.data.frame()
intern_standard <- intern_standard[!is.na(intern_standard$POS), ]
rownames(intern_standard) <- intern_standard$abbreviation

#'generate calcualte formula
intern_standard$mass <- calculateMass(intern_standard$formula)
intern_standard$mz <- mapply(intern_standard$mass,
                             intern_standard$POS,
                             FUN = mass2mz)

#' Fit for each standards
intern_standard$mzmin <- intern_standard$mz - 0.02
intern_standard$mzmax <- intern_standard$mz + 0.02
intern_standard$rtmin <- intern_standard$RT - 15
intern_standard$rtmax <- intern_standard$RT + 15
```

```{r EIC_extract_for_internal_standard2, eval=FALSE}
#' Extract the EICs
eics <- chromatogram(lcms1[idx_qc],
                     mz = as.matrix(intern_standard[, c("mzmin", "mzmax")]),
                     rt = as.matrix(intern_standard[, c("rtmin", "rtmax")]),
                     chunkSize = 10)

rownames(fData(eics)) <- intern_standard$abbreviation

dr <- "EIC_IS/full/raw/"
dir.create(dr, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
for (i in seq_len(nrow(intern_standard))) {
    png(paste0(dr, "EIC_", intern_standard$abbreviation[i], ".png"),
        width = 12, height = 8, units = "cm", res = 600, pointsize = 4)
    plot(eics[i, ], main = intern_standard$name[i],
         col = paste0(col_qc, 80))
    grid()
    legend("topright", col = col_device,
           legend = names(col_device), lty = 1)
    abline(v = intern_standard$RT[i], col = "red", lty = 3)
    dev.off()
}
```

EICs show good rt reproducibility, but intensity variability between samples,
not only between groups.

### Refine identified chromatographic peaks

```{r refine1, eval=!file.exists("refine_identified_lcms1.RData")}
#' Apply on whole dataset
param <- MergeNeighboringPeaksParam(expandRt = 7, expandMz = 0.0015,
                                    minProp = 0.75)
lcms1<- refineChromPeaks(lcms1, param = param, chunkSize = 10)
chromPeakData(lcms1)$merged |>
                      table()
save(lcms1, file = "refine_identified_lcms1.RData")
```

```{r eval=file.exists("refine_identified_lcms1.RData")}
load("refine_identified_lcms1.RData")
```

We check the number of identified chromatographic peaks in all samples of a data
set can help spotting potentially problematic samples. Below we count the number
of chromatographic peaks per sample and show these numbers in a table.

```{r refine3}
#| tbl-cap: "Table 2. Samples and number of identified chromatographic peaks."
#' Count the number of peaks per sample and summarize them in a table.
data.frame(sample_name = sampleData(lcms1)$sample_name,
           peak_count = as.integer(table(chromPeaks(lcms1)[, "sample"]))) |>
    kable(format = "pipe")
```

There is a decrease of identified peaks related with injection order.

## Retention time alignment

We do an initial correspondence round on the QC samples. The alignment will be
based on the features shared in these samples.

```{r rt_alignment_1, eval=!file.exists("align_lcms1.RData")}
#| fig-cap: "Figure 5. Initial correspondence analysis."
# Initial correspondence analysis
param <- PeakDensityParam(sampleGroups = sampleData(lcms1)$device == "QC",
                          minFraction = 1,
                          binSize = 0.01, ppm = 10,
                          bw = 2)
lcms1 <- groupChromPeaks(lcms1, param = param)
```

```{r rt_alignment_2, eval=!file.exists("align_lcms1.RData")}
#' Define parameters of choice
subset <- which(sampleData(lcms1)$device == "QC")
param <- PeakGroupsParam(minFraction = 0.9, extraPeaks = 50, span = 0.5,
                         subsetAdjust = "average",
                         subset = subset)

#' Perform the alignment
lcms1 <- adjustRtime(lcms1, param = param)
```

```{r rt_alignment_3}
#| fig-cap: "Figure 6. Retention time alignment results."
#' Visualize alignment results
plotAdjustedRtime(lcms1, col = paste0(col_sample, 80), peakGroupsPch = 1, cex.lab = 1.2)
grid()
legend("topright", col = col_device,
       legend = names(col_device), lty = 1, bty = "n", horiz = TRUE)
```

```{r rt_alignment_4, eval=!file.exists("align_lcms1.RData")}
#' Get data before alignment
lcms1_raw <- dropAdjustedRtime(lcms1)

#' Apply the adjusted retention time to our dataset
lcms1 <- applyAdjustedRtime(lcms1)

# Save aligment object 
save(lcms1, file = "align_lcms1.RData")
```

```{r eval=file.exists("align_lcms1.RData")}
load("align_lcms1.RData")
```

Another interesting information to look a the the distribution of these features
along the retention time axis.

```{r correspondence_3}
#| tbl-cap: "Table 5. Distribution of features along the retention time axis."
# Bin features per RT slices
vc <- featureDefinitions(lcms1)$rtmed
breaks <- seq(0, max(vc, na.rm = TRUE) + 1, length.out = 15) |>
    round(0)
cuts <- cut(vc, breaks = breaks, include.lowest = TRUE)

table(cuts) |>
    kable(format = "pipe")
```

The results from the correspondence analysis are now stored, along with the
results from the other preprocessing steps, within our `XcmsExperiment` result
object.

This data frame provides the average *m/z* and retention time (in columns
`"mzmed"` and `"rtmed"`) that characterize a LC-MS feature. Column, `"peakidx"`
contains the indices of all chromatographic peaks that were assigned to that
feature. The actual abundances for these features, which represent also the
final preprocessing results, can be extracted with the `featureValues()`
function:

```{r feature_abundance}
#'Extract feature abundances
# featureValues(lcms1, method = "sum") |>
#    head()
```

We can note that some features (e.g. F0002) have missing values in some samples.
This is expected to a certain degree as not in all samples features,
respectively their ions, need to be present. We will address this in the next
section.

## Gap filling

```{r gapfilling1}
#' Percentage of missing values
sum(is.na(featureValues(lcms1))) /
    length(featureValues(lcms1)) * 100
```

Gap filling: 40%.

we could find different features between plasma vs blood and between devices.
(background noise???)

```{r gapfilling2, , eval=!file.exists("gapfilling_lcms1.RData")}
#' Fill in the missing values in the whole dataset
lcms1 <- fillChromPeaks(lcms1, param = ChromPeakAreaParam(), chunkSize = 10)
save(lcms1, file = "gapfilling_lcms1.RData")
```

```{r eval=file.exists("gapfilling_lcms1.RData")}
load("gapfilling_lcms1.RData")
```

```{r gapfilling3}
#' Percentage of missing values after gap-filling
sum(is.na(featureValues(lcms1))) /
    length(featureValues(lcms1)) * 100
```

The gap-filling rescue up to 2% Missing Value. When we go back to the raw data,
we rescue intensities that were measures for specific features. If there is no
intensity, it will no be filled and then we will need to do imputation in PCA.

```{r}
lcms1_noblanks <- lcms1[sampleData(lcms1)$device!="BLANK", keepFeatures = TRUE]
```

NOTE: when subsetting lcms1 object: use \[\], do not use coma, add keepFeatures
= TRUE to avoid removing feature definition.

```{r Detected-vs-filled-signal1}
#Distribution of data 

layout(mat = matrix(1:2, ncol = 1), height = c(0.5, 0.5))
par(mar = c(4, 4, 1, 2))

# A. DISTRUBTION in ALL SAMPLES. 

#' Get only detected signal in all samples
vals_detect <- featureValues(lcms1, filled = FALSE)
#' Get detected and filled-in signal
vals_filled <- featureValues(lcms1)
#' Replace detected signal with NA
vals_filled[!is.na(vals_detect)] <- NA
#' Identify features with at least one filled peak
has_filled <- is.na(rowSums(vals_detect))
#' Calculate row averages for features with missing values
avg_detect <- rowMeans(vals_detect[has_filled, ], na.rm = TRUE)
avg_filled <- rowMeans(vals_filled[has_filled, ], na.rm = TRUE)
#' Plot the values against each other (in log2 scale)
plot(log2(avg_detect), log2(avg_filled),
     xlim = range(log2(c(avg_detect, avg_filled)), na.rm = TRUE),
     ylim = range(log2(c(avg_detect, avg_filled)), na.rm = TRUE),
     pch = 21, bg = "#00000020", col = "#00000080",  
     xlab = "log2(avg_detected)"
     )
grid()
abline(0, 1)

# B. DISTRIBUTION IN ALL SAMPLES WITHOUT BLANK

#' Get only detected signal in samples without blanks
vals_detect_noblank <- featureValues(lcms1_noblanks, filled = FALSE)
#' Get detected and filled-in signal
vals_filled_noblank <- featureValues(lcms1_noblanks)
#' Replace detected signal with NA
vals_filled_noblank[!is.na(vals_detect_noblank)] <- NA
#' Identify features with at least one filled peak
has_filled_noblank <- is.na(rowSums(vals_detect_noblank))
#' Calculate row averages for features with missing values
avg_detect_noblank <- rowMeans(vals_detect_noblank[has_filled_noblank, ], na.rm = TRUE)
avg_filled_noblank <- rowMeans(vals_filled_noblank[has_filled_noblank, ], na.rm = TRUE)
#' Plot the values against each other (in log2 scale)
plot(log2(avg_detect_noblank), log2(avg_filled_noblank),
     xlim = range(log2(c(avg_detect_noblank, avg_filled_noblank)), na.rm = TRUE),
     ylim = range(log2(c(avg_detect_noblank, avg_filled_noblank)), na.rm = TRUE),
     pch = 21, bg = "#00000020", col = "#00000080",
     xlab = "log2(avg_detected)"
)
grid()
abline(0, 1)

```

The detected (x-axis) and gap-filled (y-axis) values for QC samples are highly
correlated. Especially for higher abundances, the agreement is very high, while
for low intensities, as can be expected, differences are higher and trending to
below the correlation line. Below we, in addition, fit a linear regression line
to the data and summarize its results

```{r lr}
#' fit a linear regression line to the data
l <- lm(log2(avg_filled) ~ log2(avg_detect))
summary(l)
```

Note about linear regression: the linear regression line has a slope of 0.42 and
an intercept of 5.09. This indicates that the filled-in signal is on average
0.42 higher than the detected signal (which means half of the detected signal).

# Data Normalization

## Initial quality assesment

PCA: unsupervised visualization. We need to impute first all missing values
(replaced by numbers from a uniform distribution)

```{r Impute_MV}
#' Impute missing values using an uniform distribution
na_unidis <- function(z) {
    na <- is.na(z)
    if (any(na)) {
        min = min(z, na.rm = TRUE)
        z[na] <- runif(sum(na), min = min/2, max = min)
    }
    z
}

#' Row-wise impute missing values and add the data as a new assay
tmp <- apply(assay(res, "raw_filled"), MARGIN = 1, na_unidis)
assays(res)$raw_filled_imputed <- t(tmp)

```

Before plotting the PCA, we apply a log2 transform, center and scale the data.
The log2 transformation is applied to stabilize the variance while centering to
remove dependency on absolute abundances.

```{r PCA_all}
#| fig-cap: "PCA of all samples colored by device."
# General PCA: blanks, QCs and devices
#' Log2 transform and scale data

vals <- assay(res, "raw_filled_imputed") |>
    log2() |>
    t() |>
    scale(center = TRUE, scale = TRUE)

#' Perform the PCA
pca_res <- prcomp(vals, scale = FALSE, center = FALSE)

#' Plot the results
vals_st <- cbind(vals, device = res$device)
pca_12 <- autoplot(pca_res, data = vals_st , colour = 'device', scale = 0) +
    scale_color_manual(values = col_device)
pca_34 <- autoplot(pca_res, data = vals_st, colour = 'device',
                   x = 3, y = 4, scale = 0) +
    scale_color_manual(values = col_device)
grid.arrange(pca_12, pca_34, ncol = 1)
```

PCA: Blank separates from the samples. Plasma and Blood separates from devices.
PC1 represents 51.97% variance and PC2 20.46%. QCs are not as grouped as
expected.

(autoplot gives automatically colors. No need to define specific colors)

In this line, we are subsetting the res object to do not take into account
blanks and/or QCs.

i.e. this line should be for xcms exp object:: blank \<-
res\[sampleData(res)$device == "BLANK", keepFeatures = TRUE]
    this line should be for summarise exp object:: res_blank <- res_full[, res_full$device
== "blank"\] keep feature == TRUE: is to avoid that the description of the
features is removed. Only in xcms experiments.

### RLA

An RLA value is the abundance of a feature in a sample relative to the median
abundance of the same feature across multiple samples.

-   Within group RLA plots: assess tightness of replicates within groups should
    have a median close to zero and low variation around it.
-   across groups, they allow to compare behavior between groups

```{r RLA-log-abundance-all}

        border = col_sample, boxwex = 1,
        outline = FALSE, xaxt = "n", main = "Relative log abundance",
        cex.main = 1)

legend("topright", col = col_device,
       legend = names(col_device), lty=1, lwd = 2, xpd = TRUE, ncol = 3,
       cex = 0.8,  bty = "n")

#change legend for sample_name
```

### Noise Comparison

Below we compare the noise signals between devices. We first calculate the
overall signal in the dataset and then calculate the signal that is in the
chromatographic peaks detection. We then subtract the two to get the noise
signal.

```{r Noise_comparison, echo=FALSE}
# overall signal in the dataset 
#' - for each file calculate the sum of intensities 
background  <- spectra(lcms1[!idx_blank_qc]) |>
    split(fromFile(lcms1[!idx_blank_qc])) |>
    lapply(tic) |>
    lapply(sum) |>
    unlist()

# Overall signal that is in the chromatographic peaks detection 
detected <- apply(assay(res_sample), 2, function(x) sum(x, na.rm = TRUE))
 
# substract and plot
names(background) <- names(detected) <- res_sample$device
noise <- background - detected
 
f <- factor(names(noise), levels = unique(names(noise)))
group <- split(noise, f)
 
plot(NULL, xlim = c(1, length(group)), ylim = range(unlist(group)), 
     xaxt = "n", xlab = "Devices", ylab = "Noise", 
     main = "Noise comparison between Devices")
for (i in seq_along(group)) {
  points(rep(i, length(group[[i]])), group[[i]], pch = 19, 
col = col_sampleonly[i])
}
axis(1, at = seq_along(group), labels = names(group))
```

## Between sample normalisation

Between-sample normalization use filled-in features to effectively mitigate
variations influenced by technical issues, such as differences in sample
preparation, processing and injection methods. In this instance, we will employ
a commonly used technique known as median scaling.

### Median Scaling

This method involves computing the median for each sample, followed by
determining the median of these individual sample medians. This ensures
consistent median values for each sample throughout the entire data set.
Maintaining uniformity in the average total metabolite abundance across all
samples is crucial for effective implementation.

This process aims to establish a shared baseline for the central tendency of
metabolite abundance, mitigating the impact of sample-specific technical
variations. This approach fosters a more robust and comparable analysis of the
top features across the data set. The assumption is that normalizing based on
the median, known for its lower sensitivity to extreme values, enhances the
comparability of top features and ensures a consistent average abundance across
samples.

```{r normalization-factor-all}
#' Compute median and generate normalization factor
mdns <- apply(assay(res, "raw_filled"), MARGIN = 2,
              median, na.rm = TRUE )
nf_mdn <- mdns / median(mdns)

#' divide dataset by median of median and create a new assay.
assays(res)$norm <- sweep(assay(res, "raw_filled"), MARGIN = 2, nf_mdn, '/')
assays(res)$norm_imputed <- sweep(assay(res, "raw_filled_imputed"), MARGIN = 2,
                                  nf_mdn, '/')

```

```{r normalization-factor-noblank}
#' Compute median and generate normalization factor (NO BLANKS)
mdns_noblank <- apply(assay(res_noblank, "raw_filled"), MARGIN = 2,
              median, na.rm = TRUE )
nf_mdn_noblank <- mdns_noblank / median(mdns_noblank)

#' divide dataset by median of median and create a new assay.
assays(res_noblank)$norm <- sweep(assay(res_noblank, "raw_filled"), MARGIN = 2, nf_mdn_noblank, '/')
assays(res_noblank)$norm_imputed <- sweep(assay(res_noblank, "raw_filled_imputed"), MARGIN = 2,
                                  nf_mdn_noblank, '/')
```

### Assessing overall effectiveness of the normalisation approach

#### Principal component analysis

The evaluation will be performed by comparing the distribution of the log2
transformed feature abundances before and after normalization.

```{r PCA-normalisation, fig.height=7, fig.width=7}
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: PCA after normalization of all samples colored by device.

#' Data before normalisation
vals_st <- cbind(vals, device = res$device)
pca_raw <- autoplot(pca_res, data = vals_st,
                    color = 'device', scale = 0) +
    scale_color_manual(values = col_device) +
    labs (title = "PCA before Normalization", tag = "A")
#' Data after normalization
vals_norm <- apply(assay(res, "norm"), MARGIN = 1, na_unidis) |>
    log2() |>
    scale(center = TRUE, scale = TRUE)

pca_res_norm <- prcomp(vals_norm, scale = FALSE, center = FALSE)
vals_st_norm <- cbind(vals_norm, device = res$device)
pca_adj <- autoplot(pca_res_norm, data = vals_st_norm,
                    color = 'device', scale = 0) +
    scale_color_manual(values = col_device) +
    labs (title = "PCA before Normalization", tag = "B")
grid.arrange(pca_raw, pca_adj, ncol = 1)
```

Now all devices group together, and PCA2 change (plasma -\> devices, now devices
-\>plasma).

```{r PCA-normalisation-noblank, fig.height=7, fig.width=7}

#| fig-cap: PCA after normalization of all samples without blanks colored by device.

#' Data without blanks before normalisation
vals_noblank_st<- cbind(vals_noblank, device = res_noblank$device)
pca_noblank_raw <- autoplot(pca_res_noblank, data = vals_noblank_st,
                    color = 'device', scale = 0) +
    scale_color_manual(values = col_device) + 
    labs (title = "PCA before Normalization (no blank)", tag = "A")

#' Data without blanks after normalization
vals_noblank_norm <- apply(assay(res_noblank, "norm"), MARGIN = 1, na_unidis) |>
    log2() |>
    scale(center = TRUE, scale = TRUE)
pca_res_noblank_norm <- prcomp(vals_noblank_norm, scale = FALSE, center = FALSE)


vals_noblank_st_norm <- cbind(vals_noblank_norm, device = res_noblank$device)
pca_noblank_adj <- autoplot(pca_res_noblank_norm, data = vals_noblank_st_norm,
                    color = 'device', scale = 0) +
    scale_color_manual(values = col_device) +
    labs (title = "PCA before Normalization (no blank)", tag = "B")

grid.arrange(pca_noblank_raw, pca_noblank_adj, ncol = 1)
```

Normalisation have an impact in PC1 improving the grouping of QCs, Plasma and
Blood samples.

#### CV after normalisation

```{r CV-after-norm}
#' Calculate the CV values
index_samples <- res_noblank$device %in% c("WHATMAN", "MITRA", "CAPITAINER", "PLASMA", "BLOOD")
index_QC <- res_noblank$device == "QC"

sample_res <- cbind(
    QC_raw = rowRsd(assay(res_noblank, "raw_filled")[, index_QC],
                    na.rm = TRUE, mad = TRUE),
    QC_norm = rowRsd(assay(res_noblank, "norm")[, index_QC],
                     na.rm = TRUE, mad = TRUE),
    Study_raw = rowRsd(assay(res_noblank, "raw_filled")[, index_samples],
                       na.rm = TRUE, mad = TRUE),
    Study_norm = rowRsd(assay(res_noblank, "norm")[, index_samples],
                        na.rm = TRUE, mad = TRUE)
)

#' Summarize the values across features
res_noblank_df <- data.frame(
    QC_raw = quantile(sample_res[, "QC_raw"], na.rm = TRUE),
    QC_norm = quantile(sample_res[, "QC_norm"], na.rm = TRUE),
    Study_raw = quantile(sample_res[, "Study_raw"], na.rm = TRUE),
    Study_norm = quantile(sample_res[, "Study_norm"], na.rm = TRUE)
)

kable(res_noblank_df, format = "pipe")
```
